summary.text: Bayes' theorem is a rule for inverting conditional probabilities, so the probability of a cause can be found from its effect.
For example, it finds the chance a patient has a disease given a positive test, using the chance that the test is positive when the disease is present.
One of its applications is Bayesian inference, where it turns the probability of observations given a model into the probability of the model given the observations.

paragraphs.heading: Turning a probability around
paragraphs.text: Bayes' theorem, also called Bayes' rule or Bayes' law, is a rule for flipping a conditional probability around. A conditional probability is the chance of one thing given that another is true. The theorem lets you go from the chance of an effect given its cause to the chance of the cause given the effect. Thomas Bayes worked it out in the 18th century, and Pierre-Simon Laplace found it independently.

paragraphs.heading: A medical test
paragraphs.text: Picture a doctor testing a patient for a disease. The patient has it or not, and the test comes back positive or negative. A positive result for someone who is sick is a true positive; a positive result for someone who is healthy is a false positive. Bayes' theorem uses how often the test is positive when the disease is present to find how likely a patient with a positive test is to have the disease.

paragraphs.heading: The pieces of the formula
paragraphs.text: In words, the theorem says: the chance of A given B equals the chance of B given A, times the chance of A, divided by the chance of B. It only works when P(B) is not zero. P(A | B), the chance of A given that B is true, is called the posterior probability. P(B | A) is the reverse, the chance of B given A, and can be read as a likelihood. P(A) and P(B) are the plain chances of A and B with no conditions, and P(A) is often called the prior, meaning before the new evidence.

paragraphs.heading: Where it comes from
paragraphs.text: The rule follows from how joint and conditional probabilities fit together. The chance that A and B both happen, written P(A ∩ B), equals the chance of A given B times the chance of B. By the same logic it also equals the chance of B given A times the chance of A. Setting those two products equal and dividing by P(B) gives Bayes' theorem. When the possibilities are split into A and not-A, written ¬A, the bottom of the fraction becomes a sum of just two terms, one for each case.

paragraphs.heading: Bayes and Price
paragraphs.text: Thomas Bayes was a minister, statistician and philosopher. After he died, his family passed his papers to his friend Richard Price. Price edited the manuscript for two years, then sent it to John Canton, who presented it to the Royal Society in December 1763. His essay, which contains the theorem, was published in Philosophical Transactions in 1763. Price wrote its introduction and chose one of the two solutions Bayes gave. Some argue it should really be called the Bayes–Price rule, but using Bayes's name alone is now too settled to change.

paragraphs.heading: Laplace and later
paragraphs.text: Working separately from Bayes, Laplace used conditional probability to connect an updated posterior with a prior, given evidence. He repeated and extended Bayes's results in 1774, seemingly unaware of them. Much later, Sir Harold Jeffreys put the theorem on a formal footing of axioms. He wrote that it is to probability theory what the Pythagorean theorem is to geometry.

paragraphs.heading: Learning from data
paragraphs.text: One of the theorem's many uses is Bayesian inference, a way of doing statistics. It takes the probability of what you observed given a model of the world and turns it into the probability of that model given what you observed. When the theorem is written in terms of odds, a quantity called the Bayes factor appears. It shows up in Alan Turing's work of the early 1940s, where he called it the factor in favour of a proposition.
